newsitem.title: USA: New AIDS drugs therapies cost effective?.
newsitem.headline: New AIDS drugs therapies cost effective?.

text.p: The high cost of AIDS drugs, which can run around $15,000 a year, might be offset at least in part by savings from keeping patients healthy and out of the hospital, new studies suggested on Thursday.

The studies do not give any definitive estimates of costs or savings. No one yet knows how long people will have to stay on the new combination drug therapies, whether the drugs will suppress the virus indefinitely, or whether the prices will drop in the coming years.

But the studies on hospitalization frequency and length of stay, combined with some anecdotal evidence of empty beds in AIDS wards around the country, suggest that the drug price tag is only part of the story.

Despite some federal efforts to make the drugs available to more people, advocates have complained that some HIV-infected people still face delays, waiting lists or even lotteries to get life-prolonging medications.
The data was presented on Thursday at the Fourth Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, a major five-day gathering of AIDS researchers.

In one study, Dr. Ramon Torres, director of the AIDS Center at St. Vincents Hospital in New York's Greenwich Village neighborhood, the number of patients needing hospitalization declined even though the number of patients seeking treatment rose by 21 percent.

From 1995 to 1996, the monthly average number of hospitalized patients declined by 24 percent, from 104 to 79 and the average length of stay dropped by 16 percent, from 15 days in May 1995 to 12.6 days in March 1996.

Torres said he did not have any firm data on overall costs but added "As we make decisions regarding access to these treatments, especially for the poor, we must keep in mind the immense financial, physical and emotional costs of a serious AIDS-related hospitalization and balance those with the price of potent therapies that we know can help reduce those costs."
In a study in Los Angeles, Dr. Peter Ruane of Tower Infectious Disease Medical Associates saw similar trends.

The new drug therapies led to declines in hospital admissions, length of stay, skilled nursing days and referrals to out-patient specialists for radiation therapy and treatment of serious skin, intestinal and eye disorders.
They have even cut home care referrals. "In the last six months of 1994, we had 65 people on home care. Now we have five," Ruane said.

Before the conference opened this week, a number of activists and doctors that are part of the AIDS Healthcare Foundation lamented the ongoing problems in drug access. Although the number of states' assistance programs covering new protease inhibitor has risen, some do not cover the full cost or give people access to all the available drugs.
So far there are three protease inhibitors on the market, and some people do better on one version than on another.

"It is imperative that federal, state and local funding catch up with the AIDS treatment advances of the last year so that all patients may enjoy equal access to this new-found hope," said Michael Weinstein, president of the foundation.
